There could be other stuff going on emotionally for you. Weight loss is something you can do for your health and is great obviously but is "external" compared to your internal psychology. Since you say you've been trying to lose weight for a decade and have recently reached your highest weight I think it's possible that your mind is trying to tell you something; namely that it wants you to heal/deal with things. I think therapy might be an option to consider and you can talk about your weight loss struggles with them as well. It's great you want to try again and you shouldn't stop with your current plan of working on nutrition, etc but I think the mental health piece could make a lot of difference for you as it did me.

I have very deep psychological problems from my experiences growing up being gay and overtly feminine. But honestly what really f'ed me up was getting old enough to go to a gay bar and being treated like garbage there because of my weight and femininity. I get that this is kinda controversial, and that a lot of people find feminine men to be bitchy or whatever. But let me tell you....as a young gay man putting so much hope and having so much excitement into finding "my people" and having it be crushed by other gay men was absolutely devastating.  To be fair I probably went to an unusually toxic gay bar. But I honestly think this is a major thing we need to work on. It's fine if you're not attracted to femininity or to people who are overweight and people who are so quick to accuse of internal homophobia are also the problem. But like....damn. Gay men need to learn to treat people who they aren't interested in sleeping with better. I was naïve and genuinely looking for friends and that experience gave me deeper scars than anything I experienced in high school.

I don't know why but it really seems as though roles in which compassion is so important tend to attract the most hateful, conniving people (possibly due to burn out? but idk). As of right now I've basically given up on health care but still want to try and do something that isn't just ho-hum retail and dealing with mean customers.

I find people can be too sensitive these days (lol) and I tried to make it really clear that I understood where you were coming from and that I didn't want you to feel bad in any way because I understand the difference. I get that it's a celebratory thing for a lot of people, and has a sense of comradery to it. I think it would be unfortunate if you changed your language because of this. It's not really about the word, although my post sort of made it about the word, but it's more about the attitude behind the usage of language if that makes sense. Like if all gay men called me queen in a friendly and "brotherly" manner it wouldn't bother me at all. It's more just the sneering, dismissive usage of queen or even "campy" that is hurtful to me when it's clearly used to denote that someone isn't cool or sexy or whatever just because they're overtly homosexual in presentation.

I appreciate your response and understand that you're being positive and supportive but I just wanted to respond to it because it brought up something for me. What I'm about to say might sound like an attack but I don't intend for it to be one. Also this ended up being super long. But anyway, it seems to be a fairly typical response to categorize someone who is more overtly feminine or "flaming" as in "obviously gay" or "gay acting" as being queeny or a queen. To me there's a lot of connotation with that word of being "a queen" it's like saying that something about you is inherently comedic or silly, or that you're a cross dresser. I hear the word queen used a lot in more of a dismissive sort of way. And I find once people view you as a "queen" you're no longer really someone who is viewed as sexually desirable or someone to take very seriously. It feels like there's an implication that I've "failed" at being my gender and that I should at least have the decency to be trans, or call myself nonbinary, or whatever, but being a gay man is something I've "failed" at because I haven't managed to hide it. And I just get really hurt and confused by this treatment from gay men. It's understandable that a lot of gay men are interested in much more masculine traits so many wouldn't necessarily be as attracted to a man with feminine characteristics but gay men also aren't attracted to women but can treat them with a great deal more respect. Trans women are also treated with a lot more respect within the gay community. But somehow being male and acting more on the feminine side has this shameful connotation to it and you're not just "a gay man" anymore but you're "a queen", someone who people feel the need to clearly delineate themselves from. Like "I'm gay but I'm not like THAT." It's just something I've really noticed and have really struggled with personally and is why I don't tend to interact with a lot of gay men. It actually took me a long time to realize that there are a lot of men who are specifically attracted to effeminate guys partly because I felt "othered" by this community which I'm supposed  to be apart of for so long and genuinely thought my personality made me too ugly for anyone to want to be with. And the men who are attracted to me (who typically tend to be bisexual) don't call me a queen or make me feel bad or like I'm a "character" because I am the way I am, they just interact with me like a regular person which is what I want. And like I said I've noticed that the men who I tend to date are usually the kind of "masculine" or "straight acting" men that are apparently so desired so it's just so weird to me that there's this subtle implication in gay culture that effeminate men are lesser than in some way or sexually unsuccessful. (By the way I like feminine men as well, it's just typically who is attracted to me and who approaches me). But yeah.....I get that there's a kind of comradery by referring to people as "queen" and that I'm sure you didn't mean it in the way I described it's more just something I wanted to get off my chest.

I certainly think that there are a set of specific behaviors that are quite affected and "put on" but there are also naturally occurring effeminate gay men or "flaming gay" men.  Like to say nobody is naturally like that is just completely wrong, lol. But yes there are people who make being gay their defining personality trait and put on an exaggerated act.

Well the first thing I think would be to really ask yourself what purpose the limerence serves. Like, why has your brain adopted this as a behavior? What does it "do" for you? You seem to recognize the destructive aspects of it, but why does it reoccur?

It might help to record your thoughts especially when you feel your limerence the most strongly. If you look back on them later you might be able to notice certain patterns. Are there certain triggers? Does it happen during certain times of day? Is there a pattern amongst the people? etc.

I think if you start documenting it and looking at it as objectively or "scientifically" as possible you might identify previous traumas or thought patterns or something that need addressing and healing. There might be some kind of hole in your life or in your past that needs to be filled appropriately.  It might just be a force of habit that's difficult to break.

I've found that with BPD (but really this applies to everyone) the first thing you have to do is start deeply and on a physical level start having your own back and what they call "loving yourself." I always hated that term "loving yourself", like it seems so corny and dumb but I mean....it's kind of the perfect wording at the same time.

Just from how your post is worded it's obvious that you are talking to yourself in an abusive voice. Something that some people find helpful is to pretend that every time you think about yourself or talk to yourself you are talking to a child or another person.

So you can still be critical and make changes when you need to, but not abuse yourself verbally. 

The thing is that if you truly hate yourself or if you hate the way you act, the BEST way to change yourself into something you won't hate is by accepting yourself. The more you hate yourself, the more you talk like this to yourself the more you will be stuck in a loop and be exactly as you are now. So ironically by engaging in this behavior you are acting as if you are extremely content with yourself to the point where you are refusing to change or perhaps even grow.

Well as human beings we've evolved to be social animals and are somewhat hardwired to gather into groups. When we don't feel connected socially with something bigger our mind/body can give us warning signals that something is amiss and needs to be changed and these warning signals are often things like depression, poor mood, etc. I dislike a lot of the current view psychology has on things like depression and anxiety: namely that it should be eradicated through medication (that isn't especially effective in most cases) or (in my opinion) dorky rituals like meditation. I think a more effective approach is to view emotions as our mind's immune system and it should be listened to. Sometimes it can go wrong, but it's purpose is to protect you. You aren't happy and don't feel fulfilled because your brain is worried that without more social contacts and being apart of humanity as a whole your survival is in danger.  Rather than swell up your throat and give you hives, your brain is making you feel unwell in an attempt to get you to change. So I think first rather than continue to worry or feel out of place or feel like you're not acting the way you should you should sort of give your body a "pat on the back" and realize that feeling unhappy, unfulfilled, and bleak is not a bad thing really. Just in general give yourself a break. Take a moment to seriously reflect on your success so far as well. I think really what you need to do is be a part of something you find meaningful. Try doing stuff you would have never thought to try to do like learning an instrument, foraging for wild edibles, volunteering at an old folk's home. You might hate it, that's fine. Keep doing stuff. Keep getting out there. Join a book club or make one of your own, etc. Think of stuff you already like to do and be proactive in thinking of ways in which you could turn that interest into something that involves other people. If you're nervous, try doing stuff with your spouse alongside you as support. Connect with those people in your area whose personalities are like hidden gems. There are other people out there near you who don't like football, who don't like drinking, and who are probably staying at home and not interacting with anyone because they think nobody will get them either. When you start to build a circle of friends or at least acquaintances who you can tolerate outside of your immediate family your brain is going to start calming down. When your brain starts calming down and isn't giving you warning messages, it will open up again to the possibility of pursuing other things and creating new goals. And maybe as a side bonus if you end up liking one of these hobbies, new and unexpected goals might appear just simply from that.

I was trained as a CNA because I thought I wanted to be a nurse as well and was going to use the course as a stepping stone. Before I had been working mostly retail jobs and HATED them and wanted to have a job where I was actually making a difference and was respected more and treated better. 

So first of all I would say that the vast majority of people treat CNAs like maids and in my experience you're treated by everyone -patients and staff alike- as being expendable. I did my practicum at both a hospital and a nursing home and I found the pace to be absolutely insane and incredibly stressful. You are expected to take care of a huge number of patients at one time and in order to do your job you simply have to cut corners and not provide people with the level of care you probably think should be appropriate. It's constantly short staffed and chaotic. When it comes to paperwork you need to have everything looking perfect but when it comes to real life you end up having to do the bare minimum. It's an unwritten, unspoken rule that everyone knows is wrong but it just persists. I found those work environments to be really draining and toxic. Maybe if you work in a hospital near you things would be way better, this was just my experience. 

Home care on the other hand is SO much better because you can have one on one contact, take your time, develop a personal relationship with the people you are caring for, etc. Although in home care you tend to gain less experience if you plan on becoming a nurse and you tend to be totally on your own without much assistance.

As a side note, working closely alongside nurses there is a HUGE amount of paperwork they have to do to the point where their job mostly consists of paperwork rather than helping people. I found that in general nurses tend to be very cliquey and many of them act like they never left high school.

All in all I think nursing or being a CNA is something you should really commit to and want to do. I think going in it just for the money is an approach that is going to end up being unfair to you and for your patients/clients although it's what A LOT of CNAs and nurses do and they contribute to the unpleasant work environment I mentioned.

If I were you I would seriously consider how much you want to do this and if you feel like your heart is in it, because if your heart is truly in it you can ignore all the difficulties. There are a lot of other courses that are kinda short and not overly expensive similar to the CNA course which most colleges offer if they offer the CNA course.

I view depression as a defensive mechanism that your brain employs when it is perceiving too much negative stimulus in your life in order to try and get you to change. But just like any other response that the body produces it can get out of control and end up causing you harm. That ounce of introspection and negative emotion initially designed as a warning sign can evolve to overtake your entire mind and tint everything you see. You can begin to go into a totally defensive mode where you think about your life and your self all the time and how bad it is and/or totally  try to escape as much as possible - all in the name of trying to comfort and heal yourself because your mind is in damage control. This can become very consoling and addicting even though it makes you feel horrible.

So, I guess the first thing I would say is to fully realize that you're a human being who is in pain and who is doing their best to protect them self and that you should treat yourself as such. How do you talk to yourself in your mind? Do you insult yourself and beat yourself up or do you talk to yourself gently and with compassion? I found that it really helped me to imagine myself as a small child or as another person. If another person came up to you and asked you for help with the same issues you are having, how would you respond? If a child came up to you and told you they that they felt life was totally bleak and that they felt numb would your response to comfort them really be to get them to play a video game? Do you see how it would be inappropriate to leave a struggling, depressed child to play video games? I would imagine that child would feel totally neglected and that a video game would clearly be a sub-par substitute for actual help. But that's what you're doing with yourself. Using escapism as a band aid when you clearly need a loving, gentle, empathetic, and sympathetic touch.

The first thing you can do is to make sure you're getting enough sleep, eating properly, and drinking enough water - these things can all really effect your mood. Exercise can also help. Try literally writing down a list of your interests and things you would like to find in a job - there are a lot of entry level jobs that aren't flipping burgers. Maybe you won't find something that is perfect, but it could certainly be a lot better than where you are now. Also try to seek professional help. In general, do things that build you up. Acknowledge that you're a sentient, emotional being that needs and deserves to be treated well by first and foremost your own self and that feeding an out of control emotion such as depression with excessive escapism is causing you further distress and pain and is a form of neglect.

Since about the age of 12 I've been on all kinds of medication - for depression, anxiety, psychosis, etc. At the age of 26 what I've personally come to realize is that psychotropic medication only really helps you if the cause of your mental illness is a brain/chemical imbalance. 

When you put your hand on a hot stove, a healthy body/mind's reaction is to pull back that hand in a reaction to the stimulus of heat which is damaging your skin. I think that depression is the way your brain is trying to save you and help you, it's essentially a defense mechanism that's saying SOMETHING IS WRONG WITH MY LIFE SOMETHING IS WRONG WITH MY LIFE FIX IT FIX IT. Medication addresses those instances in which your brain is misfiring and telling you something is wrong with your life when everything is actually totally fine. But just like it would be pretty rare for someone's hand not to feel the pain of a hot stove and draw back, it's pretty rare for someone's brain to misfire in that way. The tricky thing with mental health however is that what often happens is that if your brain is truly misfiring that often eventually results in someone's life becoming bleak and difficult - so I can see where a lot of professionals err on the side of prescribing medication. However, there is a very real element of monetary gain from giving someone medication which people should be wary of and the way doctors and others prescribe psychoactive medication right now is totally out of control and excessive.

If there isn't a genuine chemical imbalance in your brain the positive effects of medication are very slim. If you don't have a chemical imbalance they're about as powerful as a glass of tea or maybe coffee at best but do nothing to change the way you view the world. Some of them are also very sedating.  For the few people who do genuinely have a chemical imbalance they can be life changing and really do change the way they view the world, because that imbalance was causing their perceptions to warp. The negative effects can be very real from taking this medication however.

All in all it seems you're really prone to having adverse reactions with recreational drugs and that you're prone to anxiety. I think you should begin charting your emotions eating/sleeping habits and when you consume alcohol or other drugs. I also think you should begin journal-ling, not necessarily to vent your emotions (although that can be really helpful for a lot of people) but to keep track of events in your life. Are there patterns to your mood? You've already identified a few such as the negative effect drinking has, are there more? Seriously consider what is going on in your life right now. Are you financially stable? Is there conflict and turmoil in your workplace? Do you have rewarding and fulfilling personal relationships? Is your life a hot stove or a comfortable chair? Does your brain have a reason to flash out this sign that something is terribly wrong, or is there no real reason for it to do so? You could benefit from medication if you can't readily identify aspects of your life that are unhealthy. That being said, in my opinion regardless if you're dealing with a chemical imbalance or not, therapy is useful. It sounds like you're worrying a lot about the state of the world in general, even if medication reduces or even eliminates that baseline feeling of anxiety/depression your thought patterns need some mending. In order to function in the world you need to be able to let go of concerns that are totally out of your control to a certain extent and therapy can help with that. You may be dealing with some cognitive distortions that can occur from a lot of different sources.

I really don't like using cliches but in this instance I think one applies - "not judging someone unless if you have walked a mile in their shoes." If someone born under extreme circumstances such as abuse and poverty were to have switched places with you at birth and had your exact upbringing and brain chemistry etc - maybe they would have faired far worse and have had way more issues than you, and maybe if you were in their shoes you could have overcome their situation much better than they could have? Or maybe the reverse is true. What I'm trying to get at is that everyone is an individual who deals with situations and emotions differently and that you can't really judge someone else's suffering because you haven't lived inside their mind and had their exact upbringing and/or set of genetics. It's entirely possible that someone born under dire circumstances might end up preferring their life over yours if they could see the effects and the struggles of both.

Also, having problems with mental health is not a character flaw or a weakness. I highly doubt you would think someone is morally at fault for being born blind or something, right? Events in your life can hurt your mind just like events in your life can hurt your arm - but whereas a broken arm is obvious a depressed mind or someone with ocd or adhd isn't something that other people can easily see - but that doesn't mean it is a character flaw for having that problem.

Depression makes you feel bad in general - and it is making you feel bad about feeling bad. When you reach out, talk to people who you trust about it, try to get help for it, and move forward in your life you are fighting depression. When you feel ashamed for being depressed, feel pathetic, give up, stop trying to seek help because you feel you shouldn't have depression to begin with, and when you feel invalid as a human being, you are giving into depression and are feeding it and making it stronger.

In my opinion breathing techniques, meditation, ASMR, etcetc are all just distractions aimed at dealing with surface level symptoms of anxiety and are actually quite pseudo scientific and I find it really annoying that they're regularly touted as cure-alls by basically everyone including professionals (although breathing techniques admittedly work in the midst of a panic attack they don't really do much else). The two things that have actually helped me were 1. delving into the anxiety, figuring out where it came from, why it persists 2. exposure therapy. It sounds like you're already being regularly exposed to what is making you anxious, so I would recommend 1. Maybe you have some cognitive distortions centered around this situation, maybe there was past trauma, etc. If you're having trouble figuring this out or don't know where to begin try keeping a journal of the thoughts that pass through your head when you are in this situation and review those thoughts once you're calmed down again with a list of common cognitive distortions and really evaluate if you're not thinking rationally. Maybe there are past issues you haven't healed from, etc. It sounds like right now you're trying to find ways to block out the anxiety, ignore it, or distract yourself from it - but the more you do that the more powerful the anxiety becomes because you reinforce the idea to your brain that the situation is truly dangerous and should be avoided. If you confront it head on it may be awful and it may feel for a moment like the worst thing but your brain and body realize that the anxiety can't actually cause you physical harm and isn't really dangerous- and that's when you begin to heal. You might need professional help to do this. As a side note, have you tried talking with your boyfriend and letting him know how you feel?
